How to use this guide

Every chapter has the same rhythm: the idea in one paragraph, the mathematics in a shaded box, the MATLAB code that implements it (copied from the project files), an "In plain words" explanation, and a "What would happen if…" box that shows why each design choice was made. The last chapters contain the complete evaluation, the A-to-Z list of improvements and more than 70 viva questions with answers.

If you only have ten minutes before the viva, read Chapter 1, Chapter 10 (why v4.1.4 failed), Chapter 11 (results) and Chapter 15 (viva).

1. The project in one chapter

1.1 The problem

BUET residential halls hand out meals against paper meal cards. Cards are shared, lost or sold to non-residents, and the queue moves slowly. We replace the card with the student's voice. At the counter the student says their Student ID (roll number) and their full name. The system must answer four questions:

  1. Who was named? Which of the enrolled students do the spoken words refer to, or nobody?
  2. Is it really them? Does the voice belong to that student, or is a friend speaking for them (an imposter, a "proxy meal")? If it is a friend, who is it?
  3. Is it live? Is a person speaking now, or is a phone playing a recording of the student (a replay attack)?
  4. May they eat? Is the student on this month's paid roster, is a meal window (breakfast, lunch, dinner) open, and have they not already eaten in this window?

1.2 Where the project came from

StageWhat it wasMain weakness
Senior baseline (Group 1, EEE'21, "Voice Based Secured Residential Hall Entrance")MATLAB script. Fixed 3 s recording at 44.1 kHz, pre-emphasis 0.99, block-energy silence removal, 12 MFCC + Δ + ΔΔ, one 8-codeword VQ codebook (LBG) per phrase. Access if the nearest ID codebook and the nearest name codebook belong to the same person.No rejection threshold: anyone saying a name was accepted as the nearest student. No noise or channel handling, no anti-spoofing, no meal logic.
Our proposal (24 July 2026)Five modifications: AGC + rational resampling, sub-200 Hz liveness, spectral subtraction, STE+ZCR endpointing, dining business logic with CSV logs.These are sound DSP ideas, but they do not decide identity robustly.
v4.1.4 (our previous release)GUI kiosk with 8 kHz processing, spectral subtraction, DTW matching, monthly roster, meal windows, admin tools.Rejected most genuine students in live use (48 of 65 logged attempts), especially on a new microphone. See Chapter 10.
v4.1.4_claude (this guide)Same GUI and business logic, plus a new verification engine (files vsd_*.m). It uses two independent kinds of evidence, names the imposter and has three anti-replay layers.Limitations are listed honestly in Chapter 14.

1.3 The solution at a glance

Two independent questions are asked of the same two recordings:

  • WHAT was said (text-dependent). The spoken ID and name are compared with every stored take of every student by Dynamic Time Warping (DTW). The distances are turned into cohort scores P_id and P_name: "how much closer is this recording to student k than to k's closest rivals?"
  • WHO is speaking (text-independent). All speech frames are scored by a Gaussian Mixture Model voice model of every student, adapted from a Universal Background Model (GMM-UBM). The log-likelihood ratios become a cohort-normalised voice score V.

A fused score picks the candidate. Gates then check each kind of evidence separately. If the words point to student X but the voice clearly belongs to another enrolled student Y, the attempt is refused as an IMPOSTER and Y is reported. Before a meal is served the student must also say three random digits shown on screen. A recording made earlier cannot contain digits chosen a second ago.

1.4 Headline results (all voices in the project folder)

98.3 %genuine students accepted, leave-one-take-out, all microphones (114/116)
90.0 %genuine accepted when enrolled on one mic and tested on others (18/20)

Under the protocol where all systems are enrolled with take 1 only, the senior baseline accepted 25.9 % of genuine students on a different microphone and v4.1.4 accepted 7.4 %. v4.1.4_claude 1.1 accepts 85.2 %, while unknown speakers fall from 15.4 % (senior) to 0.9 %. Every replayed, stale or spliced recording in the demonstration was refused.

The recordings are read from VSD_Enrollment/Train. If that folder is missing, the sibling folder ../Final project v4.1.4/VSD_Enrollment/Train is used instead. The folder contains:

  • ID/<7-digit id>/*.wav: spoken roll number takes. All takes are used.
  • Name/<id>/*.wav: spoken full-name takes.

  • ID/<id>/Adaptive/ and Name/<id>/Adaptive/: takes learnt automatically on new microphones.

2. Basics you need first

2.1 Sound as a discrete-time signal

A microphone turns air pressure into a voltage x(t). The sound card samples it every Ts = 1/fs seconds and quantises each sample, for example to 16 bits. MATLAB then holds a vector x[n] = x(nTs). Our laptops capture at fs = 44.1 kHz, the Group-2 microphone at 48 kHz, and the engine works at 8 kHz.

Sampling theorem (Nyquist–Shannon): x(t) is recoverable from x[n] if it contains no energy at or above fs/2. 8 kHz sampling → band 0 … 4 kHz. Speech formants F1–F3 (≈ 300–3500 Hz) fit inside.
Sampling is taking photographs of the wave. If you take them too slowly, a fast wave looks like a slow one (aliasing). 8000 photos per second are enough for the part of the voice that carries the words and most of the speaker's character, and this is 5.5× less data than 44 100.

2.2 How speech is produced: the source–filter model

The vocal folds make a buzz (voiced sounds, with fundamental frequency F0 ≈ 85–180 Hz for men and 165–255 Hz for women) or turbulent noise (unvoiced sounds such as s, f). The vocal tract (throat, mouth, nose) acts as a filter whose resonances are the formants. In the frequency domain:

S(ω) = G(ω) · V(ω) · R(ω) (glottal source × vocal-tract filter × lip radiation) What the computer receives: Y(ω) = S(ω) · Hmic+room(ω) + N(ω)

The words are mostly in how V(ω) changes over time. The speaker is in the average shape of V(ω) (vocal-tract length) and in G(ω). The microphone and room add H(ω), and the hall adds noise N(ω). Every block of our front-end is there to keep V and G while removing H and N.

2.3 DFT, FFT and the spectrum

X[k] = Σn=0N−1 x[n] e−j2πkn/N, k = 0 … N−1, frequency of bin k: fk = k·fs/N Power spectrum P[k] = |X[k]|² / N · dB: 10·log10(P)

The FFT computes the DFT in O(N log N). We use NFFT = 256 at 8 kHz, so each bin is 31.25 Hz wide. Only bins 0…128 (0–4 kHz) are unique for a real signal.

2.4 Short-time analysis and windows

Speech is non-stationary, but over 20–30 ms the vocal tract hardly moves. We therefore cut the signal into 25 ms frames (200 samples) every 10 ms (80 samples) and take one spectrum per frame. Cutting abruptly (a rectangular window) smears energy into every bin (spectral leakage). A Hamming window tapers the edges:

w[n] = 0.54 − 0.46·cos(2πn/(N−1)), n = 0 … N−1 first side-lobe: rectangular −13 dB, Hamming −43 dB; main-lobe width: rectangular 4π/N, Hamming 8π/N

2.5 Digital filters, the z-transform and pole–zero plots

FIR: y[n] = Σk bk x[n−k] ⇔ H(z) = Σk bk z−k (only zeros, always stable, can be linear-phase) IIR: y[n] = Σ bk x[n−k] − Σ ak y[n−k] ⇔ H(z) = B(z)/A(z) (poles must lie inside |z| = 1) Frequency response: H(ejω) = H(z)|z=ejω, ω = 2πf/fs

The project uses FIR filters throughout: the pre-emphasis filter 1 − 0.97z−1, the delta (differentiator) filter, the polyphase anti-alias filter inside resample, and the loudspeaker simulator's Butterworth band-pass in the tests.

2.6 A little probability: Gaussians, likelihood and the log-likelihood ratio

N(x; μ, σ²) = (2πσ²)−½ exp(−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)); diagonal d-dimensional: product of d such terms Likelihood of frames x1…T under a model λ (frames assumed independent): p(X|λ) = Πt p(xt|λ) Log-likelihood ratio: LLR = (1/T) Σt [ln p(xt|student) − ln p(xt|everyone)]
A likelihood says how well a model explains the data. On its own it is meaningless, because a long or noisy recording makes every likelihood small. A ratio against a reference ("people in general") cancels those shared effects, so LLR > 0 simply means "this sounds more like the student than like an average person on this microphone".

2.7 Error rates used to judge a biometric system

TermMeaningOur protocol
GAR (genuine acceptance rate) = 1 − FRRFraction of genuine attempts accepted as the right studentLOTO, cross-mic, transaction sweep
FRR (false rejection rate)Genuine attempts refused. This is what annoyed students with v4.1.4.1 − GAR
FAR (false acceptance rate)Attempts by a non-owner that are acceptedUnknown speaker, perfect mimic
Wrong-student acceptA genuine student accepted as someone elseReported for every genuine protocol
EERThreshold where FAR = FRR (one-number summary)The FAR/FRR figure in §6.2

3. The front-end: from microphone samples to features (vsd_frontend.m)

Every recording is processed once by U = vsd_frontend(x, fs, c). This applies to live captures, stored templates, digits and challenge answers alike, so all comparisons are made on identical terms. The output U contains Content (features for the word match), Speaker (features for the voice model), SpeechSec, RawRms, ClipFrac and the 8 kHz audio.

3.1 Rational resampling to 8 kHz

44.1 kHz → 8 kHz: 8000/44100 = 80/441 = L/M (gcd = 100) 48 kHz → 8 kHz: 1/6 Up-sample by L (insert L−1 zeros) → low-pass H(ejω) with cut-off ωc = π/max(L, M) and gain L → keep every M-th sample Polyphase implementation: only the output samples that are kept are ever computed (cost ∝ output length)
function y = vsd_resample(x, fsIn, fsOut)
if fsIn == fsOut, y = x; return; end
g = gcd(round(fsOut), round(fsIn));
p = round(fsOut)/g;  q = round(fsIn)/g;      % 80 and 441 for a laptop mic
y = resample(x, p, q);                       % polyphase FIR, Kaiser window
y = y(:);
We need to go from 44 100 to 8 000 samples per second. This is not a whole-number ratio, so we "stretch by 80, smooth, keep 1 in 441". The smoothing low-pass filter removes everything above 4 kHz first. Without it, a hiss at 6 kHz would fold down and appear as a fake 2 kHz component.
Naive decimation (x(1:5:end), about 8.8 kHz with no filter): energy between 4.4 and 22 kHz aliases into the speech band, and fricatives such as s in "Sindid" turn into broadband noise over the formants. fs = 4 kHz: the band ends at 2 kHz, so F3 and much of F2 are lost, and names such as "Samin" and "Sindid" become hard to tell apart. Staying at 44.1 kHz: 5.5× more samples to process, and 5.5× longer frames in samples, with no gain for 26 mel bands below 4 kHz.

3.2 DC removal and spectral subtraction

Speech and hall noise add: y = s + n. The speech is non-stationary, while fans, crowd hum and hiss change slowly. So we estimate the noise power spectrum and subtract it:

Frames: 32 ms periodic Hann, 50 % overlap-add (the Hann windows sum to 1). Ym[k] = FFT of frame m Noise estimate: P̂N[k] = mean of |Ym[k]|² over the 10 % of frames with the least total energy Gain: Gm[k] = max( 1 − α·P̂N[k] / |Ym[k]|², β ), α = 2 (over-subtraction), β = 0.02 (floor) Ŝm[k] = √Gm[k] · Ym[k] (phase kept) → inverse FFT → overlap-add
[~, order] = sort(sum(Pw, 1));                    % frames from quietest to loudest
q  = order(1:max(3, round(c.SSNoiseFrac * nF)));  % quietest 10 %
Pn = mean(Pw(:, q), 2);                           % noise power per bin
G  = max(1 - c.SSAlpha * Pn ./ max(Pw, 1e-20), c.SSBeta);
yf = real(ifft(F .* sqrt(G), N, 1));              % then overlap-add
Every recording contains a little silence. The quietest tenth of the recording tells us what the room sounds like. We remove twice that much from every frame (α = 2), but never more than 98 % of a frame's power (β = 0.02 keeps a faint floor so no "musical noise" chirps appear). The proposal's 0.5 s pre-roll idea is kept for the live capture, and this version also works on stored files that have no pre-roll.
α = 1: residual noise stays in the pauses, so the speech mask keeps more non-speech frames. α = 4: weak consonants are deleted along with the noise. β = 0: isolated spectral peaks survive between gaps as "musical noise" that DTW treats as content. The noise estimated only from a fixed first 0.5 s: if a student starts talking early, the "noise" is speech and the first word is cancelled. This happened with some archived takes.

3.3 Peak normalisation and pre-emphasis

y ← y / max|y| (level independence, the proposal's AGC idea; CMVN later removes what remains) Pre-emphasis: yp[n] = y[n] − 0.97·y[n−1] ⇔ H(z) = 1 − 0.97 z−1 (zero at z = 0.97, pole at z = 0) |H(ejω)|² = 1 + 0.97² − 2·0.97·cos ω → −30.5 dB at DC, +5.9 dB at 4 kHz (≈ +6 dB/octave over the speech band)
y = [y(1); y(2:end) - c.PreEmph * y(1:end-1)];     % c.PreEmph = 0.97
No pre-emphasis: the spectral tilt of voiced speech (−6 dB/oct) lets F1 dominate every mel band. F3 and F4, which carry vocal-tract length (speaker) and place of articulation (words), are weighted about 10–20 dB lower in the cepstrum. 0.99 instead of 0.97: nearly identical above 300 Hz. The difference is below 200 Hz, which is why the proposal's sub-200 Hz liveness test must use the raw native-rate signal.

3.4 Framing, power spectrum, mel filter bank, log and DCT (MFCC)

Frames: N = 200 samples (25 ms), hop H = 80 (10 ms), Hamming window, NFFT = 256 → Pt[k] = |Xt[k]|²/N Mel scale: mel(f) = 2595·log10(1 + f/700). 26 triangles with centres equally spaced in mel between 100 and 3800 Hz Filter-bank energies: Et[m] = Σk Bm[k]·Pt[k], m = 1…26 Cepstrum (DCT-II): ct[n] = √(2/M) Σm=1M ln Et[m] · cos(πn(m − ½)/M), n = 0…12 Lifter: ct[n] ← ct[n]·(1 + (L/2)·sin(πn/L)), L = 22. c0 (overall loudness) is discarded; c1…c12 are kept
idx = (1:N) + H * (0:nf-1)';                    % [nf x N] sample indices of every frame
w   = 0.54 - 0.46 * cos(2*pi*(0:N-1)/(N-1));    % Hamming
fr  = y(idx) .* w;
S   = fft(fr, c.NFFT, 2);
P   = abs(S(:, 1:c.NFFT/2+1)).^2 / N;           % power spectrum, 129 bins
B   = vsd_melbank(c.NumMel, c.NFFT, c.Fs, c.MelLowHz, c.MelHighHz);
me  = P * B.';                                  % 26 band energies per frame
logm = log(max(me, 1e-12));
cc  = logm * vsd_dct(c.NumMel, c.NumCep).';     % c0..c12
cc  = cc .* (1 + (c.Lifter/2) * sin(pi * (0:c.NumCep-1) / c.Lifter));
For each 25 ms slice: measure how much energy falls into 26 ear-like bands, take the logarithm (as loudness perception does), then describe the band pattern with 12 numbers (the DCT is a compact "shape code"). Low cepstral coefficients describe the broad envelope, which is the vocal tract. The log is the key step: it turns multiplication by the microphone response into addition (3.6).
Filters up to 7000 Hz at 8 kHz (the senior setting at 44.1 kHz): above 4 kHz there is nothing at 8 kHz, so the empty bands produce ln(0) and garbage. The upper edge must stay below Nyquist, which is why we use 3800 Hz. Keeping c0: the features then encode how loud the student spoke, so standing closer to the mic changes the match. 20 cepstra instead of 12: tried and measured. Cross-mic acceptance fell from 78.3 % to 52.2 %, because the high cepstra encode fine spectral detail (pitch harmonics, microphone ripple) rather than the vocal tract.

3.5 Speech mask and deltas

Frame log-energy et = ln Σm Et[m]; keep frame t if et > maxt et − 3.0·ln 10 (i.e. within 30 dB of the loudest frame) Delta (regression over ±2 frames): Δct = Σn=12 n·(ct+n − ct−n) / (2·Σ n²) = [2(ct+2−ct−2) + (ct+1−ct−1)]/10

The delta is an FIR filter along time with impulse response [2, 1, 0, −1, −2]/10, a smoothed differentiator. Its DC gain is 0, so any constant offset (such as a microphone's cepstral offset) disappears from Δc.

No speech mask: 2–5 s of silence around a 1.3 s name dominate the DTW path, and every recording "matches" every other in the silent parts. A 60 dB floor: breath and room noise are kept. A 10 dB floor: weak final consonants ("-d" in Sindid) are cut. The senior code's block silence remover (4096-sample blocks kept only if above the mean energy) cuts at block edges, often in the middle of a syllable.

3.6 CMVN: the mathematical reason the system survives a microphone change

Microphone + room = LTI filter: Yt(ω) = Xt(ω)·H(ω) Filter-bank energies (H nearly constant inside one band): EYt[m] ≈ |Hm|²·EXt[m] Log: ln EYt[m] = ln EXt[m] + ln|Hm|² → DCT is linear: cYt = cXt + h, h does not depend on t Cepstral mean subtraction: cYt − (1/T)ΣτcYτ = cXt + h − ( (1/T)ΣτcXτ + h ) = cXt − mean(cX) ✔ h cancels exactly Variance normalisation: divide each dimension by its standard deviation → also cancels a gain on the dynamics
st = cc(:, 2:end);                       % c1..c12
d1 = vsd_delta(st, c.DeltaN);            % deltas
cs = st(speech, :);  ds = d1(speech, :); % speech frames only
content = [cs ds];                       % 24-D word features
mu = mean(content, 1);  sd = std(content, 1, 1);
U.Content = (content - mu) ./ sd;        % CMVN
U.Speaker = [(cs - mean(cs,1)) ./ std(cs,1,1), ds ./ std(ds,1,1)];   % voice features
v4.1.4 had cepstral mean subtraction switched off by its frozen calibration file (mfcc.CmsNormalise = 0). The microphone term h then stayed inside every frame, so a new microphone raised the distance to every template at once. This is root cause 2 in Chapter 10.
CMS only, no variance normalisation, on the voice features: measured cross-microphone voice identification falls to 60.9 % (with CMVN: 78.3–91.3 %). CMVN over a very short utterance (< 0.3 s): the mean itself becomes content-dependent. This is why a minimum of 0.35 s of speech per phrase is enforced (c.MinSpeechSec).

4. Matching the words: DTW and cohort scores

4.1 Dynamic Time Warping

The same student never says "two two zero six one four seven" at the same speed twice. DTW finds the best monotone alignment between the query frames a1…n and the template frames b1…m:

local cost d(i, j) = ‖ai − bj‖2 (24-D Euclidean) D(0,0) = 0, D(i, j) = d(i, j) + min{ D(i−1, j−1), D(i−1, j), D(i, j−1) } Sakoe–Chiba band: only |i − j| ≤ w, w = max(⌈0.4·max(n, m)⌉, |n − m| + 1) distance = D(n, m) / K, K = number of cells on the optimal path (average mismatch per aligned frame pair)

v4.1.4 divided by n + m. Dividing by the real path length K makes the distance the mean frame mismatch, so a 1 s name and a 3 s roll number are on the same scale. Ties are broken in favour of the diagonal step, as in the Python prototype.

Fast implementation: one anti-diagonal at a time (vsd_dtw.m)

C = sqrt(max(sum(A.^2,2) + sum(B.^2,2).' - 2*(A*B.'), 0));   % all local costs at once
for s = 2:(n + m)                               % cells with i + j = s
    iLo = max([1, s - m, ceil((s - bw)/2)]);    % stay inside the band
    iHi = min([n, s - 1, floor((s + bw)/2)]);
    I = (iLo:iHi)';  J = s - I;
    x1 = D(kD);  x2 = D(kU);  x3 = D(kL);       % diagonal, up, left predecessors
    useD = (x1 <= x2) & (x1 <= x3);  useU = ~useD & (x2 <= x3);
    best = x3; best(useU) = x2(useU); best(useD) = x1(useD);
    D(kC)  = C(I + (J - 1) * n) + best;         % whole diagonal in one vector step
    Lp(kC) = lp + 1;                            % path length bookkeeping
end
dist = D(R, m + 1) / max(pathLen, 1);
Every cell on the anti-diagonal i + j = s depends only on the two previous anti-diagonals. So MATLAB can fill a whole anti-diagonal in one vector operation instead of a double for loop. There are n + m interpreted steps instead of n·m, with an identical result (checked against the Python prototype: 6.3311052297 in both).

4.2 Multi-template matching and cohort normalisation

dk = min over all usable takes of student k of DTW(query, take) (v4.1.4: only take 1.wav) P(k) = ln [ mean of the 5 smallest dj, j ≠ k / dk ]

Why the ratio works: a new microphone, a louder room or a cold multiplies all distances by roughly the same factor γ. Then P(k) = ln(γ·rivals / γ·dk) = ln(rivals / dk) does not change. A fixed threshold on raw dk (v4.1.4 used 31.35 and 30.35) fails as soon as γ > 1.

function P = cohort_lower(d, k)             % in vsd_score_query.m
for c = 1:numel(d)
    o = d([1:c-1, c+1:end]);  o = sort(o(isfinite(o)));
    P(c) = log(mean(o(1:min(k,numel(o)))) / max(d(c), 1e-9));
end
P_name = +0.17 means "your name recording is e0.17 ≈ 1.19 times closer to your own takes than to the average of your five closest rivals". Negative means someone else is closer.
Band 0.1 instead of 0.4: a student who says his name 40 % slower than at enrolment cannot be aligned, and the distance explodes. No band: pathological paths (one query frame matched to half the template) become legal and imposters get cheaper matches. Cohort size 1 (ratio to the single best rival): very noisy, because one lucky rival decides. Cohort size 31 (all students): the normaliser is dominated by distant students and becomes insensitive. Mean over templates instead of min: an old take from a different mic pulls the genuine score down.

5. Who is speaking: GMM-UBM voice biometrics (vsd_gmm.m)

5.1 Gaussian mixture model

p(x | λ) = Σk=1K wk · N(x; μk, diag σk2), K = 64, x = 24-D speaker feature frame ln [wk N(x; μk, σk2)] = ln wk − ½ Σd ln(2πσkd2) − ½ Σd (xd − μkd)2/σkd2 ln p(x|λ) computed stably with the log-sum-exp trick: m + ln Σk exp(Lk − m), m = maxk Lk

Each Gaussian roughly models one class of sounds (a vowel region, a fricative, a nasal) as this speaker produces it. The mixture as a whole describes the speaker's "sound space", independent of what was said.

5.2 Universal Background Model trained by EM

E-step: γt(k) = wkN(xt; μk, σk2) / Σj wjN(xt; μj, σj2) (responsibility of component k for frame t) M-step: nk = Σt γt(k), wk = nk/T, μk = Σ γt(k)xt / nk, σk2 = Σ γt(k)xt2/nk − μk2 + 10−3

The UBM is trained on the isolated digits of all students (up to 80 000 frames). This is text-independent speech that never contains a test phrase. Initialisation is deterministic: K frames spread evenly over the data, then 10 k-means iterations, then 30 EM iterations. So MATLAB and Octave give the same model every time.

5.3 MAP adaptation: one model per student from 10–20 s of speech

nk = Σt γt(k), Ek[x] = Σt γt(k) xt / nk (student's frames, UBM responsibilities) αk = nk / (nk + r), r = 16 μ̂k = αk Ek[x] + (1 − αk) μkUBM (weights and variances shared with the UBM)
function mu = map_adapt(X, ubm, r)
L  = log_joint(X, ubm.w, ubm.mu, ubm.var);   % T x K log(w_k N(x_t))
m  = max(L, [], 2);
P  = exp(L - m);  P = P ./ sum(P, 2);        % responsibilities gamma_t(k)
n  = sum(P, 1).';                            % soft counts n_k
Ex = (P.' * X) ./ max(n, 1e-10);             % E_k[x]
a  = n ./ (n + r);                           % data-dependent adaptation factor
mu = a .* Ex + (1 - a) .* ubm.mu;

5.4 The voice score

LLR(k) = (1/T) Σt [ ln p(xt | λk) − ln p(xt | UBM) ] (frames of the ID and the name together) V(k) = LLR(k) − mean of the 5 largest LLR(j), j ≠ k (cohort normalisation, like P)
The UBM is "an average student on these microphones". The LLR asks: "does this sound more like student k than like an average student?" Subtracting the best rivals then asks: "…and more like k than like anyone else enrolled?" V > 0 for student k means k is the best voice.
K = 8 (as in v4.1.4): each Gaussian must cover several sound classes, so speakers blur together. K = 32: measured cross-mic acceptance 65.2 % (K = 64: 78.3 %). K = 128: the same accuracy as 64 but twice the cost. r = 0: pure maximum-likelihood means from 10 s of data, which over-fit and are unstable. r → ∞: every student equals the UBM, so all LLRs are 0. The UBM trained on the ID/name phrases: the test phrase is inside the "background", so LLRs shrink. Adding the digits to each student's model: tried; no gain (97.4 % LOTO either way).

6. The decision: fused score, imposter identification, unknown speaker (vsd_decide.m)

6.1 The rule

F(k) = 0.5·Pid(k) + 1.0·Pname(k) + 0.25·V(k) candidate c = argmaxk F(k) (or the typed ID) G1 quality: both phrases ≥ 0.35 s of speech and level ≥ 10−3 G2 phrase: Pname(c) ≥ 0.07 and Pid(c) ≥ −0.15 G3 voice: V(c) ≥ 0 and c is the rank-1 voice G4 imposter: X = argmax(Pid + Pname) (words), Y = argmax V (voice). IMPOSTER if Y ≠ X, V(Y) − V(X) ≥ 0.15, V(Y) ≥ 0.20 → report Y CLEAR WINNER (v1.1): also VERIFIED if F(c) − F(rank 2) ≥ 0.08, Pname(c) ≥ 0.12, voice rank of c ≤ 3, V(c) ≥ −0.10, Pid(c) ≥ −0.15 UNKNOWN if max V < 0 and max Pname < 0.07; otherwise RETRY with the failing gate named
F = c.WeightID*Pid + c.WeightName*Pn + c.Lambda*V;
[~, order] = sort(F, 'descend');  cidx = order(1);
[~, vorder] = sort(V, 'descend'); vrank = find(vorder == cidx, 1);
[~, X] = max(Pid + Pn);                 % who the WORDS name
Y = vorder(1);                          % whose VOICE it is
R.Gates.Phrase = (Pn(cidx) >= c.MinPname) && (Pid(cidx) >= c.MinPid);
R.Gates.Voice  = (V(cidx) >= c.MinVoice) && (vrank <= c.VoiceRankMax);
isImp = (Y ~= X) && (V(Y) - V(X) >= c.ImpGap) && (V(Y) >= c.ImpMinVoice);
cw = Pn(cidx) >= c.ClearWin.MinPname && R.FMargin >= c.ClearWin.MinFMargin && ...
     vrank <= c.ClearWin.VoiceRankMax && V(cidx) >= c.ClearWin.MinVoice;   % v1.1
if isImp
    R.Decision = 'IMPOSTER';  R.ImposterSuspect = st{Y};
elseif (R.Gates.Phrase && R.Gates.Voice) || cw
    R.Decision = 'VERIFIED';            % R.Rule = 'standard' or 'clear-winner'
elseif max(V) < c.MinVoice && max(Pn) < c.MinPname
    R.Decision = 'UNKNOWN';
else
    R.Decision = 'RETRY';               % Stage 'phrase' or 'voice' tells the user what to fix
end

6.2 Why these weights and thresholds

  • The ID phrase gets half weight and only a veto (−0.15; it was −0.10 in v1.0). All roll numbers start with "2206…", so their DTW distances are nearly equal (see the score distributions below). A positive requirement on Pid would reject genuine students at random.
  • The name carries the word evidence (threshold 0.07). Names differ a lot between students.
  • The voice must be rank 1, unless the candidate is a clear winner (Section 6.5). This is what stops a friend who says your roll number and name perfectly.
  • λ = 0.25 for V in F. V is on a larger numerical scale (genuine median about 1.3) than P (about 0.4). The weight keeps the words in charge of choosing the candidate, while the gates make both kinds of evidence necessary.
  • The thresholds were selected on the corpus under the constraint "0 unknown speakers accepted", maximising genuine acceptance (LOTO + cross-mic) (proto/tune2.py). They were then frozen and checked in MATLAB/Octave.

6.3 Worked example 1: the student v4.1.4 kept rejecting (2206147)

Take 4 of 2206147 was recorded on our laptop microphone. It was held out of the enrolment and scored against all 32 students:

Score2206147Best other studentThresholdGate
P_id+0.052 (DTW 4.79)+0.033 (2206143, DTW 4.86)≥ −0.15passed
P_name+0.167 (DTW 4.66)−0.012 (2206137, DTW 5.42)≥ 0.07passed
V (voice)+0.259 (rank 1)+0.178 (2206138)≥ 0, rank 1passed
Words X / voice YX = 2206147, Y = 2206147no conflict

Result: VERIFIED, then the random-digit challenge "six six zero" was answered correctly (distance 4.19, margin 1.05), in the same voice. In v4.1.4 the same take had an ID margin of about 1.02 (limit 1.20) and was refused at the first gate.

6.4 Worked example 2: an imposter is named

2206147 says 2206141's roll number in his own voice (built from his own digits) and plays a recording of 2206141's name. Real output of RUN_ME('demo'):

  Candidates (fused score = 0.5*P_id + P_name + 0.25*V):
    #1 2206141  P_id +0.010  P_name +22.458  voice +0.227
    #2 2206147  P_id +0.187  P_name -0.263  voice +0.757
* IMPOSTER ALERT: the spoken ID/name claim student 2206141, but the VOICE belongs
  to enrolled student 2206147 (voice score 0.76 vs 0.23). Access refused.
=> IMPOSTER 2206141 (likely imposter 2206147)
The words say "2206141". The voice says "2206147", with a gap of 0.53, more than the 0.15 required. The system therefore does not simply refuse: it tells the hall office who was probably speaking. (P_name = +22 is so large because the name was a digital copy of a stored file. Had the phrases been accepted, the replay memory would have caught it next.)
ImpGap = 0: any genuine student whose voice happens to be ranked 2nd would be labelled an imposter. That is unfair and would cause queue arguments. ImpGap = 0.5: a friend with a similar voice could pass the imposter check (they would still fail the voice gate G3). No voice gate (words only): measured unknown-speaker acceptance rises from 0 % to 6.0 %. No word gate (voice only): 100 % of unknown speakers are accepted, because some enrolled voice is always the closest. Cohort-normalised scores are relative, so the words are needed to reject strangers.

6.5 v1.1: the "clear winner" rule, and why we did not just lower the threshold

At the counter, a genuine student (2206141) was refused twice by the old v4.1.4 matcher even though the name phrase ranked him first both times. The log showed:

v4.1.4 logTry 1Try 2
ID phrase best match22061572206144
Name phrase best match22061412206141
Name lead (runner-up ÷ best distance)1.2091.194
Required fixed margin1.2121.212
Joint margin for 22061411.13×1.09×
DecisionREFUSED: "ID and Name acoustic matches disagree"REFUSED

Two things went wrong. The ID phrase is a near-tie for every student (all roll numbers start with 2206), so its top-1 was a random other student and it vetoed a correct name. And the name, which did point to the right student, missed a fixed margin by only 0.3 % and 1.5 %. The same pattern refused many students.

There were two ways to respond, and both were measured on the same trials (Python mirror of the engine, enrolment from take 1 only, 85 genuine / 117 unknown-speaker / 3627 perfect-words imposter trials):

OptionGenuine acceptedUnknown speaker acceptedPerfect-words imposter accepted
v1.0 rules91.8 %0.9 %0.08 %
A. Lower the name threshold 0.07 → 0.0591.8 %3.4 % (2.6 % with all takes enrolled)0.08 %
B. Relax the ID veto −0.10 → −0.1592.9 %0.9 %0.08 %
C. Clear-winner ranking rule94.1 %0.9 %0.25 %
v1.1 deployed = B + C95.3 %0.9 %0.25 %
Lowering a threshold helps everybody who is close to it, including strangers: option A accepted no extra genuine student but let 2.6–3.4 % of unknown speakers in. A clear winner is different: it asks whether rank 1 is far ahead of rank 2 on the fused score, with a strong name match and a voice that is at least in the top three. A stranger never produces a large lead for one enrolled student, so the stranger rate does not change.
VERIFIED (clear winner) ⇔ F(c) − F(rank 2) ≥ 0.08 ∧ Pname(c) ≥ 0.12 ∧ voice rank(c) ≤ 3 ∧ V(c) ≥ −0.10 ∧ Pid(c) ≥ −0.15 ∧ ¬ IMPOSTER

The old v4.1.4 matcher (still used when params.vsd.Enable = false) received the same idea as a relative rescue in speaker_verification_decision.m: accept when the name ranks the candidate first with a lead ≥ 1.12 over the runner-up (and ≥ 1.15 over the mean of the 5 nearest), the joint margin is ≥ 1.08, the candidate's ID distance is within 12 % of the best ID distance, the fused normalised distance is ≤ 1.60 (the ordinary ceiling is 1.15), and the voice ranks him in the top three. Both refused tries above clear the lead and joint-margin tests (1.209 and 1.194 ≥ 1.12; 1.13 and 1.09 ≥ 1.08).

Lead 0.04 instead of 0.08: more near-ties are accepted, and imposter acceptance rises further. Voice rank ≤ 5: a friend with a similar voice could ride on a correct name. No Pname floor: a clear lead built only from the roll number (which is nearly identical for everyone) would be accepted. The cost we accepted: the perfect-words imposter rate rose from 0.08 % to 0.22 % in MATLAB/Octave (0.25 % in the Python mirror).

6.6 Field log: an imposter the old matcher let in, and how v4.1.4_claude stops it

In a counter test, 2206147 said 2206150's roll number and name in his own voice. The old v4.1.4 matcher (the Final project v4.1.4 folder) served him breakfast as 2206150:

Old matcher logValue
Joint rank 1 / rank 22206150 1.13 / 2206163 1.21 (lead only 1.07×)
ID phrase best match2206158 (2206150 only rank 3)
ID / name distance vs fixed limit32.15 / 31.35 and 35.56 / 30.35, both above
DecisionVERIFIED 2206150: a meal served to an imposter

That matcher compares only the words. Anyone who says the right roll number and name looks like the owner to it. The voice model it had (8 Gaussians trained on one take) was too weak to object.

The v4.1.4_claude engine scores the voice as well. Each of 2206147's four held-out takes was scored as if its words were a perfect match for 2206150 (the mimic protocol of Section 11):

2206147 takeV(2206150)Best voiceDecision
1 (database mic)−0.82 (rank 28)2206147, +1.36IMPOSTER → 2206147
2 (database mic)−0.85 (rank 28)2206147, +1.40IMPOSTER → 2206147
3 (database mic)−0.84 (rank 28)2206147, +1.47IMPOSTER → 2206147
4 (laptop mic)−0.46 (rank 16)2206147, +0.26IMPOSTER → 2206147

The voice gap V(Y) − V(X) is at least 0.72, far above the 0.15 needed. Even when V(Y) falls below 0.20 and the IMPOSTER label is not printed, the voice gate (rank ≤ 3, V ≥ −0.10) still refuses the claim.

The legacy matcher inside v4.1.4_claude (used only when params.vsd.Enable = false) now has the same protection: capture_voice_features.m keeps the raw recording, and vsd_voice_veto.m scores it with the GMM-UBM models before any meal is served. Tested on the stored files, it refused 2206147 → 2206150 and 2206141 → 2206150 on all four takes each and named the speaker. It passed every genuine take of 2206150 and 2206147.

How to tell which engine you are running: every transaction in v4.1.4_claude starts with the line Engine: v4.1.4_claude-1.1 …. Lines such as "Multi-modal joint biometric ranking" and "39-dimensional MFCC features" without an Engine line come from the old folder.

7. Replay-attack prevention: three layers

Threat model. An attacker wants a meal in another student's name. The attacker can:

  • (a) speak the student's ID and name themselves (the imposter case of Chapter 6);
  • (b) play a recording of the student from a phone;
  • (c) inject a stored enrolment file digitally;
  • (d) cut and paste the student's recorded digits to answer a challenge.

A replay of the real student has the right words and the right voice, so the identity gates alone cannot stop it. Liveness needs something a recording cannot know in advance.

7.1 Layer 1: the random-digit challenge (vsd_challenge.m)

After the identity is verified, the kiosk shows and speaks three random digits, for example "four seven two". The answer is checked in three ways.

Reference: T(code) = the claimed student's own isolated digit recordings joined in that order (0.2 s lead and tail, 0.05 s gaps, each at unit peak) Decoys: the 27 codes that differ from the asked code in exactly one position (3 positions × 9 other digits), which are the hardest confusions Dreq = DTW(answer, T(code)), Dj = DTW(answer, T(decoyj)) Content pass: Dreq ≤ 5.40 and margin = minj Dj / Dreq ≥ 0.97 Voice pass: gap = maxj Vch(j) − Vch(claimed) < 0.40 (GMM-UBM on the digit frames) Splice guard: Dreq < 2.00 → the answer is a paste-up of the stored digit files → REPLAY
codes = [code; neighbours(code)];            % asked code + 27 decoys
for k = 1:size(codes,1)
    T = template(M.Digits{sidx}, codes(k,:), c);   % own digits concatenated
    D(k) = vsd_dtw(U.Content, T.Content, c.DtwBand);
end
info.Margin = min(D(2:end)) / max(D(1), 1e-9);
pass = (D(1) <= c.Challenge.MaxDist) && (info.Margin >= c.Challenge.MinMargin);
info.Splice = D(1) < c.Challenge.MinDist && strcmp(info.Mode, 'own');
if info.Splice, pass = false; end
Measured on the corpusResult
Genuine answers, digit content (72 trials, connected counting takes vs isolated templates)93 % pass per attempt (67/72)
Genuine answers, voice gap < 0.40 (54 trials, 18 speakers)90.7 %; another student speaking the digits: 1.9 %
Replayed ID / name recordings offered as the answer0 / 18
Recording of an older code0 / 18
Smallest distance of a genuine live answer3.58 (so the splice floor 2.0 never refuses a genuine answer)
End-to-end sweep (one transaction per student, two codes allowed)16 of 17 testable students passed
A recording made yesterday cannot contain "four seven two" if the kiosk chose those digits one second ago. Comparing against the 27 codes that differ by one digit makes the test strict: the answer must be more like the asked code than like every near-miss. Checking the voice of the digits stops a trick where the victim's recording plays the ID and name and the attacker then speaks the digits himself.
One digit only: a 10 % chance that an old recording happens to contain it, and too short for a reliable voice check. Six digits: stronger, but the pass rate falls (each digit is another chance to fail) and the queue slows. No decoys, only Dreq ≤ threshold: any clear speech in the student's voice would pass, including an old code. A fixed phrase instead of random digits: it can be recorded once and replayed forever. No splice guard: an attacker with the enrolment files could paste "four", "seven", "two" together and pass with distance ≈ 0.01. The demo's case 7 shows this being caught.

7.2 Layer 2: replay memory, the digital-copy detector (vsd_replay_guard.m)

flag if min over { all stored takes of the claimed student, last 20 accepted live takes } of DTW(query, take) < 1.0

Two natural repetitions are never identical. The smallest DTW distance between two genuine takes on the corpus was 2.41, while an injected copy of a stored file scores 0.00. Accepted utterances are remembered in VSD_ReplayMemory.mat (features only, no audio), so a recording of today's accepted transaction cannot be reused tomorrow.

7.3 Layer 3: the proposal's sub-200 Hz liveness heuristic (advisory)

ratio = Σ20–200 Hz |X(f)|² / Σ20–3800 Hz |X(f)|² on the native-rate recording; advisory flag if ratio < 2.4·10−4

Small phone loudspeakers cannot reproduce frequencies below about 200 Hz. The ratio is computed, logged and shown, but it does not refuse on its own. A microphone change moves it too, and there is no labelled corpus of real loudspeaker replays to calibrate it. Refusing students on an uncalibrated test would repeat v4.1.4's mistake.

"Why is your proposal's sub-200 Hz test only advisory?" Because a measurement you cannot calibrate must not make decisions. We replaced it with a test whose security rests on information, not on acoustics: a recording cannot know a random code.

8. Enrolment, the model cache and self-adaptation

8.1 Building the models (vsd_build_models.m, vsd_models.m)

  1. List every WAV under ID/, Name/ (including Adaptive/) and Digits/.
  2. For each file, a cache key path | bytes | date is built. Only new or changed files are passed through vsd_frontend, and features are cached inside VSD_Models.mat.
  3. A take is skipped if it is too quiet (RMS < 10−3) or too short (< 0.35 s of speech). The build reports each skip, for example Name/2206136/12.wav (too quiet/short: rms 0.0027, speech 0.23s).
  4. The UBM is trained from the pooled digit frames and reused as long as the digit set and the configuration are unchanged.
  5. One MAP-adapted model is built per student from all of their ID + name takes.
  6. Before every transaction, vsd_models lists the folders (a few ms). If anything changed (Enrol tab, import, digit recorder, self-adaptation), the models update incrementally.

The first build on a new PC processes all 554 files (117 ID, 117 name, 320 digit recordings) in roughly one minute. Later starts load in about one second.

8.2 Self-adaptation to a new microphone (vsd_adapt.m)

Some transactions are verified with a large safety margin: Pname ≥ 0.12, V ≥ 0.30, and the challenge passed. Their ID and name recordings are stored in ID/<id>/Adaptive/ and Name/<id>/Adaptive/. Three adaptive takes per phrase are kept, and older ones move to Adaptive/archive (never deleted, for audit). The next transaction therefore already knows how the student sounds through the counter's current microphone.

Adaptation only happens after a passed challenge and with large margins. A replayed or imposter recording therefore cannot slowly "poison" a student's profile. Without these conditions, an attacker who once got lucky would be enrolled as the victim.

8.3 Recording the digits

Admin → Open DSP workspace → Enrol tab → type the Student ID → Record digits 0-9 (vsd_enrol_digits.m). Each digit is recorded once with the same auto-stop capture and a quality check (≥ 0.15 s of speech), and saved as Digits/<id>/<id>_<word>_NN.wav. Students 2206135, 2206148 and 2206149 currently have no digits, so their challenge uses the digits of their three closest voices ("cohort" mode), which is weaker.

9. The complete transaction, the GUI and the dining rules

9.1 One counter transaction (vsd_verify_transaction.m + verify_meal_workflow.m)

  1. Capture ID (vsd_record_phrase): 0.5 s silent ambient pre-roll, a spoken 3-2-1 cue, "speak now". Recording stops 0.8 s after speech ends (8 s cap). Instant Stop works throughout.
  2. Capture name in the same way.
  3. Front-end for both (Chapter 3). A phrase with less than 0.35 s of speech → "move closer and speak clearly" (stage quality).
  4. Score the two phrases against every student (Chapters 4–5) and decide (Chapter 6). The GUI shows the top four candidates with P_id, P_name and V.
  5. Replay memory: an exact copy → REPLAY.
  6. Challenge: three random digits, up to two codes.
  7. Roster and meal (monthly_fee_entitlement, log_meal_csv): assigned this month? inside a meal window? not yet served in this window?
  8. Serve: welcome spoken aloud, MealLog.csv row, VerificationAttempts.csv row, replay memory updated, self-adaptation if confident.

9.2 What the operator sees: the six gates

GateQuestionTypical refusal text
1 Signal qualityAre both recordings long and loud enough?"The name recording is too quiet or too short (level 0.0008, speech 0.21 s)…"
2 Phrase contentDo ID + name single out one student?"REFUSED (name +0.03)": say your name clearly and retry
3 Voice biometricsIs the student the best-matching voice?"REFUSED (voice −0.12, rank 3)"
4 Imposter checkDoes the voice belong to the claimed student?Banner IMPOSTER ALERT – voice matches 2206147
5 Anti-replayFresh digits, same voice, not a copy?Banner REPLAY ATTACK BLOCKED – speak live
6 Roster and mealPaid this month, meal window open, not served yet?"NOT SERVED – 2206147: Meal time is over" / "Payment not done"

Other banners are NOT ENROLLED – access refused (UNKNOWN) and VOICE NOT VERIFIED (RETRY). The Enrol tab gains Record digits 0-9 and Rebuild voice models. The Evaluation tab can run vsd_evaluate_corpus and test_vsd_engine, and shows their CSVs.

9.3 Logs

FileOne row perColumns
MealLog.csvserved mealStudentID, StudentName, Date, Time, Meal, Method, NameDistance, CouponDistance, Margin, IDDistance, IDMargin, NameMargin
VerificationAttempts.csvattempt (accepted or refused)Time, ClaimedID, VerifiedStudent, Decision, Verified, Served, Stage, Reason, IDDistance, NameDistance, IDMargin (= P_id), NameMargin (= P_name), IDTop5, NameTop5, Engine, VoiceScore, ImposterSuspect, ReplayFlag, Challenge (new)

An old v4.1.4 attempts log with the previous header is renamed VerificationAttempts_v4.1.4.csv the first time the new version writes, so the two schemas never mix.

9.4 Dining business logic (kept from v4.1.4)

  • Monthly roster: the admin assigns enrolled IDs for the current month (Admin tab, password protected). Only assigned students are served.
  • Meal windows: MealSchedule.csv, editable in Admin → Meal hours (defaults 07:00–09:30, 12:00–14:30, 19:00–21:30, validated for overlap).
  • One meal per window: log_meal_csv looks up today's rows for the student and window (the anti-"double-dipping" rule of proposal modification 5).

If you add both "Final project v4.1.4" and "…_claude" to the MATLAB path, functions with the same name shadow each other and you may silently run the old matcher. Always start with RUN_ME from inside the _claude folder; it cleans the path first.

11. Evaluation: protocols, outputs and how to read them

11.1 The data

There are 32 enrolled students (2206131–2206164), with 117 ID takes, 117 name takes and 320 digit recordings. The recordings come from three microphones, which the evaluation infers from the file format:

  • db: the original database mic, 48 kHz stereo/float, 88 test pairs.
  • usb: a second USB microphone, 48 kHz mono int16.
  • laptop: our GUI laptop mic, 44.1 kHz.

Together, the usb and laptop microphones give 28 test pairs.

13. "What would happen if…": consolidated scenarios

Many examiners test understanding with counterfactuals. Each row gives the change, the predicted effect with its reason, and (where we measured it) the evidence.

If we……then (and why)
processed at 44.1 kHz instead of 8 kHzThe same accuracy (the mel bands stop at 3.8 kHz anyway), about 5.5× more samples to filter and frame. Frame lengths in samples change, so the FFT size must grow to 2048.
resampled with x(1:6:end) from 48 kHzAliasing: energy above 4 kHz folds into the speech band and fricatives smear. A low-pass before decimation is mandatory.
removed spectral subtractionIn a quiet room little changes. In the dining hall the noise fills the pauses, the speech mask keeps noise frames, and DTW distances rise for everyone. The cohort ratio partly compensates, but the name margin shrinks.
set α = 4 or β = 0α = 4 deletes weak consonants. β = 0 produces musical noise (isolated tonal blips) that DTW matches as if it were speech.
removed pre-emphasisF3/F4 are weighted 10–20 dB lower, speaker cues weaken and the voice gap between similar students shrinks.
used a rectangular window−13 dB side lobes: strong low harmonics leak into the higher mel bands and the cepstra become noisier.
used 50 ms framesThe spectrum smears across phonemes (the vocal tract moves within 50 ms), and DTW loses temporal resolution. 10 ms frames: too few samples for a stable spectrum (a 100 Hz pitch period is 10 ms).
kept c0Loudness enters the features, and standing 10 cm closer changes the match. This was the proposal's own complaint about the seniors.
used 20 cepstraMeasured: cross-mic acceptance fell from 78.3 % to 52.2 %, because high quefrencies encode pitch harmonics and microphone ripple.
switched CMVN off (as v4.1.4 did)The mic term h stays in the features and a new microphone shifts every distance. With CMS only on the voice features, measured cross-mic voice identification was 60.9 % (CMVN: up to 91.3 %).
dropped the deltasWords with similar static spectra but different dynamics ("one" vs "nine") become more confusable in the challenge. Deltas are also offset-free.
kept only 1.wav per studentExactly v4.1.4's failure: one session and one microphone. Take-1 other-mic acceptance: 85.2 % with the new engine (v1.1) vs 90–93 % with all takes.
used the mean DTW distance over templates instead of the minimumAn old take from another mic drags the genuine score down, and an extra take can then hurt.
set the DTW band to 0.1Tempo changes of more than 10 % cannot be aligned, so slow or fast speakers are rejected.
removed the bandDegenerate paths let a short query match a small piece of a long template, so imposters get cheaper matches and the cost rises.
used raw DTW thresholds instead of cohort scoresThe same brittleness as v4.1.4: any factor that scales all distances (mic, room, cold) moves every student across the threshold together.
simply lowered the name threshold 0.07 → 0.05Measured: no extra genuine student accepted (take-1 enrolment 91.8 % either way), but 2.6 % of unknown speakers accepted instead of 0 %. The clear-winner rule was chosen instead (+3.5 points, strangers unchanged).
demanded "ID top-1 = name top-1"Measured: LOTO 95.7 % (vs 97.4 %), cross-mic 65.2 % (vs 78.3 %), unknown FAR 13.7 % (vs 0 %) with no voice gate.
used only the voice (no words)Measured: 100 % of unknown speakers accepted. Cohort-normalised scores are relative, and some enrolled voice is always closest.
used only the words (no voice)Measured: 6.0 % of unknown speakers accepted, and a friend who knows your roll number and name is accepted.
used 8 or 32 Gaussians8: speakers blur together. 32: cross-mic 65.2 % measured. 64 is the smallest size that reached the best accuracy, and 128 adds cost with no gain.
trained the UBM on the ID and name phrasesThe test words are then "background", so genuine LLRs shrink, and the UBM changes whenever a student enrols.
set the MAP relevance to r = 0 or r = 1000r = 0: over-fitted means from a few seconds of speech. r = 1000: every student is almost the UBM, so all LLRs are ≈ 0.
set ImpGap = 0Genuine students whose voice ranks 2nd by chance are called imposters, which is unfair and embarrassing.
removed the random-digit challengeA phone recording of the student passes the identity gates. That is exactly what a replay is.
used a 1-digit or a 6-digit challenge1 digit: a 10 % chance an old recording contains it, and too short for the voice check. 6 digits: more failures for genuine users and a slower queue.
removed the 27 decoysAny clear digit string in the right voice would pass, including an old code.
removed the splice guardThe digit files themselves (for example leaked from the kiosk) could be pasted together into any code. Demo case 7 shows this.
made the sub-200 Hz test a hard gateA different microphone or a small USB mic with a weak bass response would refuse genuine students. It is uncalibrated without a replay corpus.
adapted on every accepted transactionA lucky imposter would become part of the victim's profile (template poisoning). This is why adaptation needs large margins and a passed challenge.
the student has a coldNasal resonances change. The words still match (cohort scores), and the voice score drops but usually stays rank 1. If refused, the student retries, and a confident accept adapts the profile.
the student whispersNo voicing: the voice features change completely and the speech mask keeps few frames. Refused with "speak louder". Whisper is out of scope.
two students have very similar voices (twins)V gaps become small, so the imposter check may not fire. The words still differ, but a twin who knows the words may pass. This is a known limitation of voice biometrics.
an attacker uses a speech synthesiser trained on the victimThe synthesiser can say fresh digits. This "logical access" attack is out of scope and would need a learned countermeasure (ASVspoof-style CQCC/LFCC classifiers).
the hall has 500 residentsDTW against every take grows linearly: about 5000 alignments per phrase. The fix is to pre-select the top 20 by voice score (fast) and then run DTW on those only.

14. Limitations and future work

14.1 Limitations

  • Small corpus. Only 28 genuine test pairs on non-database microphones, so the cross-mic rates carry ±10–15 % uncertainty.
  • New microphones. A student enrolled only on another microphone is accepted about 9 times in 10 at first. Self-adaptation and one enrolment take on the counter microphone close the gap.
  • Challenge cost. It adds about 3 s per student, and genuine users fail about 1 code in 6 and must say a second code.
  • Missing digits. 2206135, 2206148 and 2206149 have no digits, so their challenge is in cohort mode.
  • No real replay corpus. The replay tests use digital copies and a simulated loudspeaker.
  • Out of scope. Synthetic speech, voice conversion and skilled vocal mimicry.
  • Octave vs MATLAB. The validation was run in GNU Octave 8.4 (identical code). The GUI's new banners and six-gate table were checked by code review; a live MATLAB session should record screenshots for the report.

14.2 Future work

  • Record 1–2 takes per student on the counter microphone, and digits for every student.
  • Collect real replays (phones, Bluetooth speakers) and train a countermeasure: CQCC/LFCC + GMM, or a small CNN.
  • i-vector / x-vector embeddings with cosine scoring for large halls; voice-based pre-selection before DTW.
  • Score normalisation per microphone (Z-norm / T-norm) and noise-adaptive thresholds.
  • A Raspberry Pi kiosk with a USB microphone, and roster integration with the hall office's payment records.

15. Viva questions and answers

Answers are deliberately short, the way you would say them in the viva. Section numbers point to the full explanation.

A. Signals and sampling

Q1. What is the Nyquist rate and why is 8 kHz enough for this project?
A band-limited signal must be sampled at more than twice its highest frequency. Speech formants that carry the words and most of the speaker's identity lie below ~3.5 kHz, so fs = 8 kHz (band 0–4 kHz) suffices; telephone speech uses the same rate.
Q2. What is aliasing and how does resample prevent it?
Components above fs/2 fold back to lower frequencies after sampling. resample(x,80,441) up-samples by 80, applies a low-pass anti-alias FIR with cut-off π/441 (i.e. 4 kHz at the output), and keeps every 441st sample, so nothing above 4 kHz survives to fold.
Q3. Why is 44.1→8 kHz a rational resampling problem?
8000/44100 = 80/441 is not an integer ratio, so plain decimation is impossible; we need interpolation by L = 80 and decimation by M = 441 with one filter in between (polyphase form computes only the kept samples).
Q4. What does one FFT bin represent in our front-end?
NFFT = 256 at 8 kHz → bins spaced 8000/256 = 31.25 Hz; bins 0…128 cover 0–4 kHz.
Q5. Why frame the signal at all?
Speech is non-stationary; over 20–30 ms the vocal tract is approximately fixed, so a short-time spectrum is meaningful. 25 ms frames with a 10 ms hop give 100 feature vectors per second.
Q6. Why a Hamming window instead of rectangular?
The rectangular window's −13 dB side lobes leak strong low harmonics into higher bands; Hamming's side lobes are about −43 dB at the cost of a wider main lobe.
Q7. Is the pre-emphasis filter FIR or IIR? Where is its zero?
FIR: H(z) = 1 − 0.97z−1, zero at z = 0.97 (near DC), pole at the origin; gain −30.5 dB at DC, +5.9 dB at 4 kHz.
Q8. What is the source–filter model?
Speech = excitation (glottal pulses or noise) filtered by the vocal tract (formants) and lip radiation; in the log-spectral domain these multiply → add, which is why cepstra separate them.

B. Features

Q9. Why the mel scale?
Human pitch perception is roughly linear below 1 kHz and logarithmic above; mel(f) = 2595·log10(1+f/700). Narrow filters where formants F1/F2 need detail, wide filters where detail matters less.
Q10. Why take the logarithm of the filter-bank energies?
It compresses dynamic range like loudness perception and turns the multiplicative channel |H|² into an additive term, which CMVN can then subtract.
Q11. Why a DCT after the log?
It decorrelates the 26 correlated log-energies and compacts the envelope into a few coefficients (c1…c12), which suits diagonal-covariance GMMs and Euclidean DTW.
Q12. Why drop c0?
c0 is proportional to the overall log energy (loudness); keeping it makes the match depend on speaking distance and microphone gain.
Q13. What is liftering?
Weighting cepstra by 1 + (L/2)sin(πn/L) (L = 22) boosts the mid-order coefficients so all have comparable variance.
Q14. What exactly are delta coefficients and why is their DC gain zero?
Δct = Σ n(ct+n − ct−n)/(2Σn²), n = 1, 2 — an FIR differentiator [2,1,0,−1,−2]/10 along time. Its coefficients sum to zero, so a constant cepstral offset (a microphone) vanishes.
Q15. Derive why CMS removes the microphone.
Y = X·H → ln|Y|² = ln|X|² + ln|H|² → cYt = cXt + h (h constant). Subtracting the time mean removes h exactly. It only works for linear, time-invariant channels shorter than a frame.
Q16. What does the V in CMVN add?
Dividing by the standard deviation equalises the spread of each coefficient, removing gain on the dynamics and making Euclidean distances weight all dimensions equally.
Q17. Why is the speech mask 30 dB?
Frames more than 30 dB below the loudest frame are silence/breath; including them lets silence dominate DTW. 30 dB still keeps soft consonants.
Q18. Why estimate noise from the quietest 10 % of frames rather than a 0.5 s pre-roll?
It works for stored templates without a pre-roll and for students who speak before the cue, and it is robust because it averages many frames.
Q19. What is 'musical noise' and how does β prevent it?
Over-subtraction leaves random isolated spectral peaks that sound like tones; the floor β = 0.02 keeps a small residual everywhere so peaks do not stand out.

C. DTW and cohort scores

Q20. Write the DTW recursion.
D(i,j) = ‖ai − bj‖ + min{D(i−1,j−1), D(i−1,j), D(i,j−1)}, D(0,0) = 0; distance = D(n,m)/K with K the path length.
Q21. Why DTW instead of cross-correlation?
Speaking rate varies non-linearly within an utterance; correlation assumes a rigid shift and phase coherence. DTW warps time monotonically to align the same phonemes.
Q22. What is the Sakoe–Chiba band and why 0.4?
A constraint |i − j| ≤ w that forbids extreme warps; 0.4·max(n,m) allows ±40 % tempo differences (measured spread of our speakers) while blocking degenerate paths.
Q23. Complexity of DTW, and how did you speed it up in MATLAB?
O(n·m) cells. We vectorise along anti-diagonals (i + j = s): each depends only on the two previous diagonals, so the loop has n+m iterations of vector operations.
Q24. Why normalise by path length rather than n+m?
D(n,m)/K is the mean local mismatch per aligned pair, directly comparable between phrases of different durations.
Q25. What is a cohort score?
P(k) = ln(mean of the 5 nearest rivals' distances / dk). It measures how much closer the query is to k than to k's competitors and cancels any factor that scales all distances.
Q26. Why does the ID phrase discriminate so poorly?
All roll numbers begin '2206' and differ in 2–3 digits, so ~60 % of the utterance is identical for everyone; its DTW distances are nearly equal (e.g. 4.79 vs 4.86).
Q27. Why keep the ID phrase at all?
It still carries voice frames for the GMM, gives weak word evidence (weight 0.5), and a strongly negative Pid (< −0.15) vetoes a mismatch between the roll number and the name.

D. GMM-UBM

Q28. What is a GMM?
A weighted sum of Gaussians p(x) = Σ wkN(x; μk, Σk); with enough components it approximates any density of the speaker's feature frames.
Q29. Explain EM in two lines.
E-step: compute each component's responsibility γt(k) for each frame. M-step: re-estimate weights, means and variances as responsibility-weighted averages. Each iteration cannot decrease the likelihood.
Q30. What is the UBM and what is it trained on here?
A single 64-component GMM of 'speech in general' on our microphones, trained on the isolated digits of all students (text-independent, never a test phrase).
Q31. Write the MAP mean-adaptation equations.
nk = Σγt(k), Ek[x] = Σγt(k)xt/nk, αk = nk/(nk + r), μ̂k = αkEk[x] + (1−αk)μk, r = 16.
Q32. Why adapt only the means?
With 10–20 s of enrolment speech, variances and weights cannot be estimated reliably; mean-only MAP is the standard, robust choice (Reynolds 2000).
Q33. What does the relevance factor r control?
How many soft frames a component needs before it trusts the student's data: α = n/(n + r). Small r → fast adaptation (risk of over-fit), large r → stays near the UBM.
Q34. Why is the log-likelihood ratio better than the likelihood?
Likelihoods depend on utterance length, noise, phrase and channel; the ratio to the UBM cancels what all speakers share, leaving speaker information.
Q35. Why cohort-normalise the LLR as well?
V(k) = LLR(k) − mean of the top-5 other LLRs makes V ≥ 0 exactly when k beats his rivals and keeps the threshold stable across microphones.
Q36. Why 64 mixtures?
Measured: 32 gave 65.2 % cross-mic acceptance, 64 gave 78.3 %, 128 gave the same as 64 at double cost.
Q37. Why diagonal covariances?
After the DCT the features are nearly uncorrelated; diagonal Gaussians need 24 instead of 300 parameters per component and are numerically stable.

E. Decision and imposter identification

Q38. State the decision rule.
F = 0.5Pid + Pname + 0.25V; c = argmax F. Verified if Pname(c) ≥ 0.07, Pid(c) ≥ −0.15, V(c) ≥ 0 and c is voice rank 1, and no imposter conflict — or if c is a clear winner (next question).
Q39. What is the clear-winner rule (v1.1)?
Accept c even when its voice is only rank 2 or 3 if its fused score leads rank 2 by at least 0.08, Pname(c) ≥ 0.12, V(c) ≥ −0.10 and Pid(c) ≥ −0.15, and the imposter check did not fire. Enrolled from take 1 only, genuine acceptance rose from 91.8 % to 95.3 % with the unknown-speaker rate unchanged (0.9 %).
Q40. Why not simply lower the threshold when genuine students are refused?
A lower threshold helps everyone near it, strangers included: Pname ≥ 0.05 instead of 0.07 accepted 2.6 % of unknown speakers (all takes enrolled) and no extra genuine student. A large lead of rank 1 over rank 2 is evidence a stranger does not produce, so the clear-winner rule gains acceptance without raising the stranger rate. Its price is a higher perfect-words imposter rate, 0.08 % → 0.25 %.
Q41. How is the imposter identified?
Words claim X = argmax(Pid + Pname); voice says Y = argmax V. If Y ≠ X, V(Y) − V(X) ≥ 0.15 and V(Y) ≥ 0.20, refuse and report Y as the likely imposter.
Q42. A student said a friend's roll number and name and the old v4.1.4 matcher served him. Why, and what stops it now?
The old matcher compares only the words (DTW on MFCC) against fixed limits; the right words in any voice look like the owner. In the field log 2206147 was accepted as 2206150 on a joint score of 1.13 vs 1.21 for rank 2. The new engine adds the GMM-UBM voice: scored as perfect words for 2206150, all four of 2206147's held-out takes gave V(2206150) between −0.46 and −0.85 (rank 16–28) and V(2206147) ≥ +0.26, so the result is IMPOSTER, likely imposter 2206147. The legacy matcher in v4.1.4_claude now also has to pass this voice check (vsd_voice_veto.m).
Q43. Why require both word and voice evidence?
Measured: voice-only accepts 100 % of unknown speakers (cohort scores are relative), words-only accepts 6 % of strangers and anyone who knows your words; the fusion gave 0 %.
Q44. What is the difference between UNKNOWN and IMPOSTER?
UNKNOWN: neither the voice nor the name matches any enrolled student (a non-resident). IMPOSTER: the words claim one enrolled student but the voice clearly belongs to another enrolled student.
Q45. How were the thresholds chosen, and is that fair?
Grid search on the corpus maximising LOTO + cross-mic acceptance subject to 0 unknown speakers accepted, then frozen. The same thresholds were re-measured in MATLAB/Octave; a fresh test set would be the next step.
Q46. What does a typed Student ID change?
It fixes the candidate c = claim; every gate still applies, and if the voice belongs to someone else the result is IMPOSTER naming that person.
Q47. What was wrong with v4.1.4's decision?
It demanded that the ID phrase alone and the name alone each pass a raw distance ceiling and a margin ≥ 1.20 and agree on top-1. The ID margin was ~1.02 for everyone, so genuine students were refused at random.

F. Replay attacks

Q48. Why can't the identity gates stop a replay?
A recording of the real student has the right words and the right voice; liveness needs information the recording cannot contain.
Q49. How does the random-digit challenge work?
Three random digits; the answer is DTW-matched against the student's own digits concatenated in that order and against the 27 one-digit decoys; pass if Dreq ≤ 5.40, min decoy/Dreq ≥ 0.97, voice gap < 0.40 and Dreq ≥ 2.0.
Q50. Why the 27 decoys?
They are the hardest confusions (one digit different). Requiring the asked code to beat all of them makes the test a recognition, not just 'speech present'.
Q51. What is the splice guard?
If the answer matches the stored digit recordings too closely (D < 2.0, genuine minimum 3.58), it was pasted from those files, not spoken.
Q52. What is the replay memory?
DTW against every stored take and the last 20 accepted utterances of the student; < 1.0 means a copy (natural repeats ≥ 2.41).
Q53. Why is the sub-200 Hz test only advisory?
Its threshold cannot be calibrated without a labelled replay corpus, and a microphone change moves it; refusing on an uncalibrated test would recreate v4.1.4's false rejections.
Q54. How does the system react to a replay played through a phone speaker?
In the demo the loudspeaker distortion already failed the name gate for 2206141 (refused, RETRY); for 2206131 the phrases passed and the fresh-digit challenge refused it (REPLAY).
Q55. What attack is still possible?
A synthesiser or voice-conversion system trained on the victim that can speak fresh digits (ASVspoof logical access) — needs a learned countermeasure.

G. Evaluation

Q56. What is leave-one-take-out and why use it?
Each test take is removed from the templates and from the voice model before scoring, so the system never sees the test recording — an honest estimate with a small corpus.
Q57. Define GAR, FRR, FAR, EER.
GAR = genuine accepted; FRR = 1 − GAR; FAR = impostor/unknown accepted; EER = operating point where FAR = FRR.
Q58. What are your headline numbers?
LOTO 114/116 = 98.3 % (0 wrong-student accepts), cross-mic 18/20 = 90 %, unknown speakers 0/116, perfect-words imposters 0.22 % with 97.4 % correctly named; demo 7/7; sweep 30/32.
Q59. How did you compare fairly with the seniors?
Same recordings, same protocol (enrol take 1, test all other takes and unknown speakers): senior 87.9/25.9/15.4 %, v4.1.4 84.5/7.4/1.7 %, ours 100/85.2/0.9 % (same-mic GAR / other-mic GAR / unknown FAR).
Q60. Which modification helped most?
For the mic change: CMVN + using all takes + cohort scores; for security: adding the GMM voice gate (unknown acceptance 6 % → 0 %) and the challenge (replays 0/18).
Q61. What does the ablation show?
Only the combination of words and voice reaches 0 % unknown acceptance; the v4.1.4-style agreement rule costs genuine acceptance (95.7 % vs 97.4 % LOTO, 65.2 % vs 78.3 % cross-mic).
Q62. Why did two students fail the sweep?
2206145 missed the digit challenge twice (digits cut from a fast counting take); 2206150's held-out name take scored 0.05 < 0.07. Both would retry at the counter.
Q63. How confident are the cross-mic numbers?
Only 20–28 trials, so ±10–15 %; we state this as a tool limitation.

H. Code and MATLAB

Q64. Which file would you open to change a threshold?
vsd_config.m — every setting is there with its justification; changing front-end or GMM settings triggers an automatic model rebuild (config key).
Q65. How does the system know new recordings were added?
vsd_models lists the enrolment folders (path|bytes|date keys) before every transaction and runs an incremental update if anything changed.
Q66. How do you test without a microphone?
vsd_verify_transaction(status, p, struct('Files',…,'HoldOut',true)) or RUN_ME('demo'); the offline path uses exactly the same functions.
Q67. Why is the UBM deterministic?
Initial means are K frames spread evenly over the pooled data (linspace), then k-means and EM — no random seed, so MATLAB and Octave give the same model.
Q68. How is numerical underflow avoided in the GMM?
All likelihoods are in the log domain and summed with log-sum-exp: m + ln Σ exp(L − m).
Q69. What happens if params.vsd.Enable = false?
The v4.1.4 matcher runs unchanged (legacy fallback).

I. System, ethics and outcomes

Q70. How does the project address public health (CO4 / PO(c))?
A touchless counter replaces shared paper cards and keypads; every refusal is explained aloud and on screen.
Q71. What ethical issues arise from voice biometrics (PO(h))?
Consent, storage and retention of biometric data, the risk of accusing someone — the 'likely imposter' is a suspicion for the hall office, not proof; honest reporting of failures.
Q72. Which COs does this project map to?
CO1 PO(a),(e) DSP implementation; CO2 PO(d) theory vs experiment; CO3 PO(c),(i) filter/system design and teamwork; CO4 PO(c),(l) community problem + literature; CO5 PO(h) ethics; CO6 PO(i) team work; CO7 PO(j) report, slides, manual.
Q73. What is the sustainability benefit (PO(g))?
No printed meal cards; existing PC and microphone; incremental enrolment and self-adaptation avoid re-enrolling everyone when hardware changes.
Q74. How would you scale to 1000 residents?
Voice-score pre-selection of ~20 candidates, then DTW only on those; i-vector/x-vector embeddings; per-mic score normalisation.
Q75. What did you learn from debugging v4.1.4?
A single fixed calibration can silently disable a key step (CMS) and freeze the enrolment to one file; always measure on held-out data from the deployment microphone and look at the live logs.
